title: Adventists, Witnesses, Pentecostals
objective: After this level you can explain how the Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses and Pentecostals began in America and what sets each apart.
summary: Seventh-day Adventists grew from the Great Disappointment of 1844, Jehovah's Witnesses from Russell's Bible Students, and Pentecostals from the 1906 Azusa Street revival.

cards.headline: Three American-born movements, three distinct paths.
cards.body: One keeps a Saturday Sabbath. One goes door to door. One prays in tongues. Here's where each began.

cards.headline: The day that didn't come
cards.body: William Miller predicted Christ's Second Coming for 1843, then 1844. When it didn't come, most of his followers left, and the letdown became known as the Great Disappointment. A small group kept the hope, came to believe that Saturday, not Sunday, is the Sabbath God commanded, and organized the Seventh-day Adventist Church at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1863. Ellen G. White, who reported visions, shaped it for decades.

cards.headline: Bible students at the door
cards.body: In 1872 Charles Taze Russell founded a Bible Students movement in Pittsburgh. In 1931 it took the name Jehovah's Witnesses, from the conviction that Jehovah is God's name. Witnesses see Jesus as God's agent rather than part of a Trinity, expect a coming kingdom on earth, and are known for preaching door to door, which they call witnessing.

cards.headline: Fire on Azusa Street
cards.body: Pentecostalism spread across the nation and the world from the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles, begun in 1906. It was led by William J. Seymour, an African American minister who welcomed worshipers of every race. Pentecostals emphasize baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually shown by speaking in tongues, as at the Pentecost described in Acts.

mascot.line: Easy to blur these three. Adventists began with a date, Witnesses with Bible study, Pentecostals with a revival.

cards.headline: Adventists, Witnesses, Pentecostals: the takeaways
learned: Adventists grew from the Great Disappointment of 1844
Jehovah's Witnesses took their name in 1931
Pentecostalism spread from Azusa Street in 1906

questions.prompt: Match each leader with the movement they shaped.
questions.explanation: Ellen G. White shaped the Seventh-day Adventist Church, Charles Taze Russell founded the Bible Students movement that became Jehovah's Witnesses, and William J. Seymour led the Azusa Street revival.

questions.prompt: How did the Seventh-day Adventist Church grow out of the Great Disappointment?

options.label: Miller's prediction came true, and his movement grew quickly
Most followers stayed and set a fresh date every single year
A small group kept hope, took a Saturday Sabbath and organized
Bible students in Pittsburgh renamed their movement in 1931

questions.explanation: A small group kept its hope, came to keep Saturday as the Sabbath, and organized the church in 1863.

questions.prompt: Adventists await Christ's Second Coming, and Witnesses a kingdom on earth. Which element shared by nearly every faith do those hopes belong to?

options.label: Sacred stories of what will come at the end of time
A community's buildings and sacred objects
options.rationale: These are hopes about the future, not things.

options.label: The census count of each group's members
options.rationale: Counting isn't one of the four shared elements.

options.label: Rites of passage from one status to another
options.rationale: These hopes concern the world's future, not a life stage.

questions.explanation: Smart wrote that every faith hands down stories, including of things to come at the end of time.
